A1.justification: Both PDFs are complete, readable versions of the same SeL/AREW study. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices can be matched despite substantial expansion and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original training and evaluation results across seven tasks, including performance comparisons, AS/BT measurements, and critique-noise experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds telecom tool-use experiments, robustness tests, reward-shaping comparisons, and rubric-based evaluations.

M1.justification: The likelihood-margin objective and additive advantage correction are retained. Section 5.3 adds a tool-use adaptation of critique generation, assigning negative signals from execution failures and repetition and positive signals from newly matched expected actions.

E1.justification: v2 retains the seven original tasks and adds tau2-bench-Telecom in solo and dual-control settings. These introduce actual tool execution and coordination with a user who can perform repair actions, substantially extending coverage beyond the original query-based tasks.

E2.justification: Tables 3–4 add direct intermediate-reward shaping using the same critiques, providing an important comparison with matched supervision absent from v1. This tests the contribution of the injection mechanism itself. The original comparators remain; on-policy distillation is discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: New protocols include 7B solo and 14B dual-control telecom agents, a GPT-4o user, and a matched 70-step dual-control comparison. v2 also adds tool-error, token-use and turn metrics, GPT-5 rubric evaluation, and structured critique-corruption controls. The original seven-task settings are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds BT-only and critique-position/sign ablations, an alternative belief-elicitation prompt, false-positive corruption tests, and GPT-5 checks of proxy validity. Telecom analyses examine execution errors and reliance on user-side repair. The existing reweighting-strength analysis is relocated rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional results continue the existing point-estimate and training-curve reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 retain their values. New results include telecom rewards of 0.20 for vanilla PPO versus 0.50 for AREW under matched 70-step dual-control training, reward-shaping and corruption results, and GPT-5 AS/BT scores. Some AREW and proxy entries in Tables 3 and 5 reproduce earlier results.

T1.justification: v2 normalizes the virtual channel updates by H and H+1, revises the oracle-information assumptions through the residual-budget condition in Assumption C.6, and changes associated bounds and proofs. Appendix A also adds mathematical comparisons with on-policy distillation and direct reward shaping. These exceed notation changes.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction broaden the demonstrated scope to nine agentic tasks, including tool use, and change the headline gain from '60%' to '60-point' gains. The central claims about self-locking, coupled AS/BT bottlenecks, and AREW remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations of user-side repair dependence as a shortcut and corrupted positive critiques as inducing critique chasing. Appendices A and D explain the distinction between actor-side reweighting and changing critic targets, qualify the comparison to direct additive weak rewards, and discuss dependence on belief readouts and evaluation proxies.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access statement and telecom model, simulator, and critique-construction details. Existing hyperparameters and prompt templates are retained. However, Section 4.2 omits v1's explicit instruction to zero the auxiliary term when either positive or negative critiques are absent.

R1.justification: Appendix A substantially expands positioning relative to on-policy distillation and direct intermediate-reward shaping, distinguishing their feedback sources and objectives. New citations cover distillation, telecom evaluation, tool agents, and credit assignment; the earlier related-work discussion is largely retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries, and substantial portions of the theory and method exposition are rewritten, with more consistent AS/BT terminology and notation. v2 adds a contents section, reorganizes the appendices, and moves the reweighting-strength discussion out of the main text.

P2.justification: v2 adds telecom and robustness plots and Tables 3–5, and splits the old Figure 5 between Figure 6 and the relocated, reformatted Figure 9b. The intervention panel is correctly relabeled MediQ. New Figures 8 and 9a nevertheless contain misleading axis labels.

improvement.justification: The same-critique reward-shaping control tests the contribution of advantage reweighting, GPT-5 labeling checks dependence on the original proxies, and telecom experiments test practical tool interaction. These address important evaluation gaps in v1. Uncertainty reporting remains absent, and new axis-label errors and an omitted edge-case rule weaken reporting, but the net evidential improvement is substantial.
